steps.observation: You have 300 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
When the autumn fog rolled in thick as wool, Elias Thorn lit the lamp of Greyhaven Lighthouse the way he had for forty-three years—slowly, reverently, as though coaxing the sun into a single glass lens. Islanders said Greyhaven’s beam was as steady as Elias himself: a line of gold unbroken by storm or time.

Tonight, however, the island felt different. The sea boomed against the black rocks like a warning drum, and the wind carried a faint, unfamiliar note—a child’s laughter, distant but clear. Elias paused halfway up the spiral stairs, heart thundering louder than the surf. No children lived on Greyhaven. No one did, now that the village had dwindled to salt-streaked ruins and stories.

At the lantern room, he performed the ritual: trim wick, polish lens, check kerosene. Yet the laughter persisted, darting through the night like an echo looking for its source. Elias set his jaw, grabbed his storm coat, and descended to the cliff path.

Out on the headland stood a girl in a red raincloak, hair whip-crack wild. She faced the sea, arms outstretched, as if embracing the roaring dark. Elias approached, boots crunching gravel, but the girl didn’t flinch.

“You’ll get swept off,” he called.

The child turned. Her eyes mirrored the lantern’s glow—ancient, knowing. “I’m not afraid,” she said softly. “I came for the keeper.”

A cold shiver threaded Elias’s spine. “Who are you?”

She gestured seaward. Where the breakers churned, a phantom fleet shimmered into view: trawlers, schooners, even a rusted steamer, all long since wrecked on Greyhaven’s reefs. Their rigging glowed pale green, like moonlit bone.

“My family,” the girl whispered. “They wait.”

Realization hit Elias like a rogue wave. The tales his mother told—the legend of the Sea’s Daughters, spirits who guided drowned sailors home—were true. And tonight the sea had sent a messenger.

“But I’m still alive,” he protested.

“For now.” Sadness brushed her face. “Your light kept many from harm, but tides claim all things in turn. Come—guide one last ship.”

Down at the waterline, surf hissed over shingle. Elias felt the years weigh on his ribs: the solitude, the aching knees, the names memorized from logbooks of vessels saved. Maybe this was the reckoning—the keeper kept.

He looked back at Greyhaven’s tower, its beam revolving faithfully. Then he faced the waiting ships. Removing his cap, he bowed to the child. “Lead on.”

Hand in hand, they walked into the surf. Salt closed over his boots, his coat, his heart, yet he felt no chill—only release. The phantom fleet brightened, lanterns blooming like stars welcoming their own.

High above, Greyhaven’s lamp shone through the fog until dawn, when islanders across the channel noticed it had finally gone dark.

Weeks later, a new keeper arrived, puzzled to find the wick trimmed, the kerosene full, and a single line in the logbook: 

“Light transferred to other hands. All vessels accounted for. —E.T.”
